answer.rationale: Constraints first: rollback is off the table (compliance forbids reverting the security patch), so memory_b1's success story is inapplicable regardless of how well it worked. add_capacity (memory_b3) helped a pre-planned retail peak with lead time; we are 90 minutes into an active degradation and provisioning will not land inside this window. enable_circuit_breaker (memory_b4) contained a partner dependency failure; nothing here indicates an external dependency failing, and failing fast on the write path at settlement peak would shed exactly the customer writes the objective says to protect. That leaves regional_failover and route_read_replicas. The region-confined signature makes failover superficially the strongest match to memory_b2, but memory_b2 is an outcome-only summary that says traffic 'shifted cleanly' without stating whether the March event was write-heavy or whether replication was synchronous. Cutting over the primary during peak heavy writes is the one action that can permanently lose in-flight customer writes, which is the explicit thing we must not do. So I want the archived record for memory_b2 specifically to learn the write profile and replication mode of that event, and memory_b5 to learn whether the read-offload win was causally attributed (a real primary contention mechanism) or merely coincident with another fix. My intended action is route_read_replicas, executed as a small guarded slice (report/dashboard read traffic only, measured against primary write p99 before widening): it is reversible, it cannot lose writes, and it directly tests the plausible mechanism that peak-hour read contention on the primary is inflating write latency. Note the inherited memory is a set of successes with no recorded failures or non-adopted alternatives, so it is survivorship-biased and systematically overstates how safe each intervention is; I am treating it as hypothesis generation, not as calibrated risk. If verification shows memory_b2 covered a write-heavy event with synchronous replication and memory_b5's attribution was weak, I would escalate to regional_failover in the next window rather than now.
